messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Douglas is a 65-year-old married prosecutor of North American heritage who has spent four decades inside courtrooms, holding the state's power accountable to its citizens. He came to his first session with the careful, measured cadence of a man accustomed to building arguments, yet something in the way he paused before certain words — *police*, *crowd*, *shouting* — suggested that language itself had become treacherous territory.

The incident occurred fourteen months ago at a public demonstration Douglas attended as a private citizen, not as an officer of the court. What began as an orderly gathering deteriorated rapidly when a line of officers in riot gear advanced without warning. Douglas was caught in the surge. He was thrown against a barrier, and for what he estimates was four or five minutes — though he cannot be certain, because time fractured — he was surrounded by officers shouting commands he could not parse. The noise was overwhelming: overlapping voices, the crack of batons on shields, the static burst of radios. He could not distinguish orders from threats. He could not tell whether compliance or flight would keep him safe. By the time the crowd dispersed, he had sustained minor physical injuries, but the experience of being entirely unable to read the intentions of uniformed men with weapons — men whose authority he had spent his career respecting — had left something deeply disorganized in him.

In the weeks that followed, Douglas noticed that specific things pulled him back. The sight of a police officer — whether a colleague's escort in the courthouse corridor or a cruiser idling at an intersection — triggered an immediate surge of alarm, his body mobilizing as though the riot line were re-forming around him. Crowds producing incomprehensible overlapping voices had the same effect; he could be in the courthouse cafeteria and the moment conversation blurred into undifferentiated noise, the present moment thinned and the memory pressed through. Witnessing people behave in ways that struck him as disorderly or morally wrong — a heated argument in a parking lot, a witness losing composure on the stand — activated the same cascade, as though disorder of any kind had become a signal that danger was imminent.

When these triggers fired, Douglas's entire threat-monitoring system engaged. He had come to believe, in a way that felt irrefutable, that the world now required constant surveillance. He began watching people closely — colleagues, strangers in the gallery, the officers who testified in his cases — searching their posture and expressions for early signs of hostility. Sleep became nearly impossible; he would lie awake constructing threat assessments of the following day. At work, where he once moved through the building with the authority of long familiarity, he now found himself superalert at every turn, tracking exits and reading the room before he would sit down.

What made this worse, in ways Douglas was only beginning to understand, was that the strategies he had adopted to manage the threat monitoring were quietly feeding it. He had taken to playing loud music or the television at high volume at home, filling the auditory space so that no ambient sound could resolve into the chaotic chatter that undid him — yet the constant noise kept his nervous system elevated, so that by evening he was more sensitized, not less. He had begun asking his wife repeatedly whether she thought he seemed all right, whether his reactions were reasonable, whether she was worried about him — and though she reassured him each time, the relief lasted minutes before the doubt returned, and the need to check again grew stronger. His constant scanning of his environment — cataloguing who was near, how they were positioned, whether any of them were police — meant that he was never not looking for a threat, and the looking itself confirmed that a threat must exist. These habits, taken together, kept him perpetually primed, so that the next trigger — an officer in the corridor, a burst of indistinct voices in the gallery, a witness raising their voice — landed with full force, renewing the alarm that the strategies were supposed to quiet.

The relational cost has been significant. His wife has described feeling as though she is living with a security guard rather than a husband. His junior colleagues have noticed that he avoids pre-trial briefings with law enforcement liaisons whenever possible, delegating tasks he once performed without hesitation.

Douglas sought help after a morning when he could not enter the courtroom because two officers were conferring just inside the door. He stood in the hallway for eleven minutes. He has not told anyone at work. What he most fears is that he has become, in some permanent way, a man who cannot trust authority — which is to say, a man who can no longer do his job.
